title: Time-PEFT: Complexity-Driven Fine-Tuning for Time Series
one_liner: Use two complexity scores to predict when a time-series model needs fine-tuning, then add lightweight adapter weights to capture the hard patterns.
lead: Time-series foundation models work well zero-shot on many datasets, but sometimes they fail badly on new data because the patterns are too complex or weird. The paper gives you a recipe: measure how hard the dataset is using two scores, then if it is hard, add small adapter weights that learn just the tricky patterns without retraining the whole model.

problem.h2: When does a pre-trained time-series model need retraining?
paras: A time-series foundation model is a neural network trained on many time-series datasets (things like stock prices, sensor readings, power usage). Once trained, you can use it to forecast a brand-new dataset without retraining. Most of the time it works fine — the model has seen enough variety that it generalizes. But sometimes the new dataset is quirky: maybe the signal is noisy in an unusual way, or the channels (multiple sensors measuring different things) interact in a pattern the model never learned. Then accuracy crashes.

A naive approach: just fine-tune the entire model on the new dataset. But that is expensive — it rewrites thousands of weights and can overfit if the dataset is small. The real problem is you do not know ahead of time whether the new dataset is hard or easy. You might waste compute fine-tuning an easy dataset, or fail to fine-tune a hard one. There is no checkpoint: do I retrain or not?

callout.html: The paper gives you a rule (two complexity metrics) for deciding when to fine-tune, and a cheap way to do it (small adapter weights).

steps.text: Analyze the frequency content of each time series using spectral entropy — how spread out the signal energy is across frequencies.
Check how much information flows between channels (if you have many sensors) and whether that flow is unpredictable.
If both scores are high, the dataset has patterns the pre-trained model probably has not seen enough of.
Insert small weight matrices that learn which frequencies matter most for this dataset.
Insert small weight matrices that learn how to combine information across channels for the patterns in this dataset.

paras: The paper adds two small adapter parameter-matrices (the frequency adapter and the channel adapter) to the pre-trained model. These adapters are tiny compared to the main model, so they are fast to train. The base model stays frozen; only the adapters learn.

hidden.h2: Predicting when fine-tuning helps: complexity metrics
hidden.name: temporal complexity and multichannel complexity
paras: The paper introduces two new measurements on a dataset to predict whether fine-tuning will help, because foundation models encode common patterns (ones with simple, concentrated frequencies and stable channels) but miss rare or scattered patterns. Temporal complexity measures how spread out the signal energy is across frequencies — if most energy is in a narrow band, the signal is simple; if it is scattered everywhere, patterns are hard to spot. Multichannel complexity measures how much information crosses between channels (e.g., one sensor depends on another in hard-to-predict ways) and how much that dependence changes over time.

The insight: these two metrics predict whether fine-tuning will help. If you measure high temporal and multichannel complexity on a dataset, fine-tuning improves accuracy by 20-30%, because the adapters learn exactly the patterns the base model has not encoded — the spread-out frequencies and the channel interactions. The paper estimates these metrics from the raw time series without running the model.

heat.caption: Darker means higher complexity. Highlights show the features Time-PEFT measures.

reads.html: A complex dataset has signals that jump around across many frequencies (like static radio noise) and sensors that influence each other in ways that shift over time.
Temporal complexity is spectral entropy; multichannel complexity captures cross-channel mutual information and its non-stationarity.

mechanism.h2: Why measuring complexity lets you skip unnecessary retraining
paras: A foundation model learns shared patterns from many datasets. On an easy new dataset (simple spectral shape, stable channels), the model has already learned those patterns, so fine-tuning wastes compute. On a hard dataset (scattered frequencies, dynamic channel interactions), the model has not seen enough examples of that pattern type, so the pre-trained weights are slightly misaligned.

The paper's move: measure the dataset's complexity upfront. If it is low, skip fine-tuning and save time. If it is high, add small adapter parameters (the frequency adapter focuses on the messy frequency patterns, the channel adapter focuses on cross-sensor interactions) and fine-tune only those adapters. The adapters are so small that retraining is 10-100x cheaper than retraining the whole model, and the precision of the adapters (because they are tied to these two complexity metrics) means you hit the real improvement target — you are not guessing.

stages.s: If no: skip fine-tune, use pre-trained model as-is
If yes: attach frequency and channel adapters
Train only adapter weights on the dataset

math.words: Total error equals prediction error on the dataset plus a penalty for how much the adapters change. The penalty is scaled down so adapters can learn new patterns without being forced to match the pre-trained model's output exactly.
symbols: mean squared error: average of (predicted value minus true value) squared
a small number that controls how much you punish large adapter weights (default around 0.001)
the frequency adapter weight matrix (small, maybe 10-100 weights)
the channel adapter weight matrix (small, maybe 10-100 weights)
Frobenius norm squared: sum of all elements in the matrix, each squared (a measure of how big the matrix is)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose forecasting 10 time points, true values [2,3,1,4,5,2,3,4,2,1], model predicts [2.1,2.9,1.2,4.1,4.8,2.2,3.1,3.9,2.1,0.9].
Frequency adapter weights sum to 10 (norm squared = 100); alpha=0.001; penalty = 0.001*100 = 0.1.
Channel adapter weights sum to 8 (norm squared = 64); penalty = 0.001*64 = 0.064.
Total loss = 0.018 + 0.1 + 0.064 = 0.182. Training reduces this by improving forecasts (lowering MSE) and by keeping adapters small (lowering penalties).

math.note: The adapters learn new patterns (MSE shrinks) while staying small enough (norms stay controlled) so they do not overfit or memorize noise.

items.b: Complexity metrics do not tell the whole story.
items.html: A dataset could have high temporal complexity but still be learnable by the base model if its patterns overlap with the pre-training set. Because the metrics measure only frequency and channel structure, not other aspects like label noise or concept drift, a complex-scoring dataset might improve less than expected. Also, occasionally a low-complexity dataset improves a lot too, which means the adapters risk memorizing noise (overfitting risk) instead of learning general patterns.

items.b: Frequency and channel are not the only failure modes.
items.html: Some datasets might be hard because of unusual label noise, missing values, or regime changes (e.g., the signal's statistical properties shift mid-sequence). The adapters handle frequency and channel mixing; they will not catch every type of complexity.

If the new dataset is both complex and tiny (e.g., 50 time points), even small adapters can memorize noise instead of learning real patterns, because there is not enough data for the adapters to see the signal multiple times from different angles. The alpha penalty (the term that punishes large adapter weights) helps by making the adapters stay small, but on very small datasets you may need to raise alpha to prevent this kind of overfitting.

Validate the complexity metrics on a held-out test set. Measure whether high complexity correctly predicts high fine-tuning gain on your domain. Adjust alpha if needed. Use the adapters as a first-pass heuristic, not a guarantee.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small experiment: take a pre-trained time-series model (or train one quickly on a reference dataset). Generate or load 3-5 test datasets: some with simple spectral shapes and stable channels (low complexity), some with scattered frequencies and dynamic channel interactions (high complexity). For each dataset, compute the two complexity metrics. Then fine-tune adapters only on the high-complexity datasets and report accuracy before and after. The demo should show: (1) complexity metrics cleanly separate easy from hard datasets (because spectral entropy and channel information flow directly measure the statistical structure of the data), (2) adapters improve accuracy on high-complexity data by 20-30% (because the adapters are small enough to learn those specific patterns without overfitting, yet large enough to capture what the base model missed), (3) zero-shot accuracy on low-complexity data stays high (because the base model already knows those simpler patterns), and (4) adapter training time is 5-20% of full model retraining (because adapters have far fewer weights than the base model).
demo.metric_eq: improvement on complex datasets = (accuracy after adapters - accuracy before) for datasets where temporal complexity + multichannel complexity >= threshold
demo.closing: The metric must show that complexity metrics predict fine-tuning gain: high-complexity datasets gain 20%+, low-complexity datasets gain <5%.
